Real Analysis — 04 · The Riemann Integral

Created2026-04-20|Updated2026-04-20|Mathematics > Real Analysis
|Post View:

"The area under the curve" is a picture, not a definition. This post turns it into one. You trap the area between an upper sum that overestimates it and a lower sum that underestimates it, and call the function integrable when the trap can be closed as tightly as you like. From that single idea come proofs that every continuous function and every monotone function is integrable, a function that is not integrable (the Dirichlet function), a surprising one that is (Thomae's function), and both halves of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, the result that links this post to the derivatives of post 03. The post ends with improper integrals, Lebesgue's exact criterion for Riemann integrability, and the reason a better integral had to be invented.

Series map: 00 The Real Numbers & Completeness → 01 Sequences & Series → 02 Topology of ℝ & Continuity → 03 Differentiation & Taylor's Theorem → 04 The Riemann Integral (this post) → 05 Uniform Convergence & Power Series.

Learning Outcome

  • Define partitions, upper and lower Darboux sums, and the upper and lower integrals of a bounded function.
  • Prove the refinement lemma and deduce that every lower sum is at most every upper sum.
  • State and prove the Riemann criterion: fff is integrable if and only if U(f,P)−L(f,P)U(f,P) - L(f,P)U(f,P)−L(f,P) can be made smaller than any ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0.
  • Compute ∫01x2 dx\int_0^1 x^2\,dx∫01​x2dx from the definition, with exact upper and lower sums.
  • Prove that continuous functions and monotone functions on [a,b][a, b][a,b] are integrable.
  • Show that the Dirichlet function is not integrable and that Thomae's function is integrable with integral 000.
  • Prove linearity, monotonicity and the triangle inequality for integrals.
  • State and prove both parts of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and use integration by parts and substitution.
  • Decide convergence of the improper integrals ∫1∞x−p dx\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx∫1∞​x−pdx and ∫01x−p dx\int_0^1 x^{-p}\,dx∫01​x−pdx.
  • State Lebesgue's criterion and explain why the Lebesgue integral exists.

Chapter 1 — Partitions and Darboux sums

  • Bounded function — throughout, f:[a,b]→Rf : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}f:[a,b]→R with a<ba < ba<b and ∣f(x)∣≤B\lvert f(x)\rvert \leq B∣f(x)∣≤B for all xxx.   • Refinement — QQQ refines PPP if P⊆QP \subseteq QP⊆Q (it keeps every point of PPP and may add more). The common refinement of P1P_1P1​ and P2P_2P2​ is P1∪P2P_1 \cup P_2P1​∪P2​.
  • Local sup and inf — Mk=sup⁡{f(x):x∈[xk−1,xk]}M_k = \sup\{f(x) : x \in [x_{k-1}, x_k]\}Mk​=sup{f(x):x∈[xk−1​,xk​]} and mk=inf⁡{f(x):x∈[xk−1,xk]}m_k = \inf\{f(x) : x \in [x_{k-1}, x_k]\}mk​=inf{f(x):x∈[xk−1​,xk​]}. These exist because fff is bounded (completeness, post 00).

U(f,P)=∑k=1nMk Δxk,L(f,P)=∑k=1nmk Δxk.U(f, P) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} M_k\,\Delta x_k, \qquad L(f, P) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} m_k\,\Delta x_k. U(f,P)=k=1∑n​Mk​Δxk​,L(f,P)=k=1∑n​mk​Δxk​.

Since mk≤Mkm_k \leq M_kmk​≤Mk​, L(f,P)≤U(f,P)L(f, P) \leq U(f, P)L(f,P)≤U(f,P) for every partition. Picture tall rectangles that cover the graph and short rectangles that sit under it.

The refinement lemma

Lemma. If P⊆QP \subseteq QP⊆Q, then

L(f,P)≤L(f,Q)≤U(f,Q)≤U(f,P).L(f, P) \leq L(f, Q) \leq U(f, Q) \leq U(f, P). L(f,P)≤L(f,Q)≤U(f,Q)≤U(f,P).

Refining can only raise lower sums and lower upper sums.

Proof. By induction it is enough to add one point zzz to PPP, inside [xk−1,xk][x_{k-1}, x_k][xk−1​,xk​]. Only the kkk-th term of the upper sum changes. It is replaced by

M′ (z−xk−1)+M′′ (xk−z),M'\,(z - x_{k-1}) + M''\,(x_k - z), M′(z−xk−1​)+M′′(xk​−z),

where M′M'M′ and M′′M''M′′ are the sups of fff over [xk−1,z][x_{k-1}, z][xk−1​,z] and [z,xk][z, x_k][z,xk​]. A sup over a smaller set is no bigger, so M′,M′′≤MkM', M'' \leq M_kM′,M′′≤Mk​, and the new term is at most Mk(xk−xk−1)M_k(x_k - x_{k-1})Mk​(xk​−xk−1​). So U(f,Q)≤U(f,P)U(f, Q) \leq U(f, P)U(f,Q)≤U(f,P). The argument for lower sums is the same with infs, which can only go up. ■\blacksquare■

Corollary. For any two partitions P1,P2P_1, P_2P1​,P2​: L(f,P1)≤U(f,P2)L(f, P_1) \leq U(f, P_2)L(f,P1​)≤U(f,P2​).

Proof. With the common refinement Q=P1∪P2Q = P_1 \cup P_2Q=P1​∪P2​: L(f,P1)≤L(f,Q)≤U(f,Q)≤U(f,P2)L(f, P_1) \leq L(f, Q) \leq U(f, Q) \leq U(f, P_2)L(f,P1​)≤L(f,Q)≤U(f,Q)≤U(f,P2​). ■\blacksquare■

Upper and lower integrals

Every lower sum is a lower bound for the set of upper sums, so by completeness the following exist and satisfy L(f,P)≤∫‾f≤∫‾f≤U(f,P)L(f,P) \leq \underline{\int} f \leq \overline{\int} f \leq U(f,P)L(f,P)≤∫​f≤∫​f≤U(f,P) for every PPP:

∫ab‾f=sup⁡PL(f,P),∫ab‾f=inf⁡PU(f,P).\underline{\int_a^b} f = \sup_P L(f, P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f = \inf_P U(f, P). ∫ab​​f=Psup​L(f,P),∫ab​​f=Pinf​U(f,P).

Definition. A bounded fff is (Riemann) integrable on [a,b][a, b][a,b] if ∫ab‾f=∫ab‾f\underline{\int_a^b} f = \overline{\int_a^b} f∫ab​​f=∫ab​​f. The common value is ∫abf\int_a^b f∫ab​f or ∫abf(x) dx\int_a^b f(x)\,dx∫ab​f(x)dx.

Watch out: this is the Darboux form of the definition. The Riemann-sum form picks a sample point tkt_ktk​ in each subinterval and asks that ∑f(tk)Δxk\sum f(t_k)\Delta x_k∑f(tk​)Δxk​ tend to a limit as the mesh tends to 000. The two definitions give the same integrable functions and the same values (Bartle and Sherbert, Section 7.4). The Darboux form is easier to prove things with, because upper and lower sums do not depend on any choice of points.

Chapter 2 — The Riemann criterion and a worked example

Theorem (Riemann criterion). A bounded fff is integrable on [a,b][a, b][a,b] if and only if for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is a partition PPP with

U(f,P)−L(f,P)<ε.U(f, P) - L(f, P) < \varepsilon. U(f,P)−L(f,P)<ε.

Proof. (⇐\Leftarrow⇐) For any such PPP,

0≤∫‾f−∫‾f≤U(f,P)−L(f,P)<ε.0 \leq \overline{\int} f - \underline{\int} f \leq U(f, P) - L(f, P) < \varepsilon. 0≤∫​f−∫​f≤U(f,P)−L(f,P)<ε.

The difference is a non-negative number smaller than every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0, so it is 000.

(⇒\Rightarrow⇒) Let III be the common value and ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0. Since I=inf⁡PUI = \inf_P UI=infP​U, there is P1P_1P1​ with U(f,P1)<I+ε/2U(f, P_1) < I + \varepsilon/2U(f,P1​)<I+ε/2. Since I=sup⁡PLI = \sup_P LI=supP​L, there is P2P_2P2​ with L(f,P2)>I−ε/2L(f, P_2) > I - \varepsilon/2L(f,P2​)>I−ε/2. For the common refinement P=P1∪P2P = P_1 \cup P_2P=P1​∪P2​ the refinement lemma gives

U(f,P)−L(f,P)≤U(f,P1)−L(f,P2)<ε.■U(f, P) - L(f, P) \leq U(f, P_1) - L(f, P_2) < \varepsilon. \qquad \blacksquare U(f,P)−L(f,P)≤U(f,P1​)−L(f,P2​)<ε.■

The criterion is what you use in practice: you never compute a sup over all partitions, you exhibit one good partition for each ε\varepsilonε.

Chapter 3 — Which functions are integrable?

Monotone functions

Theorem. If fff is monotone on [a,b][a, b][a,b], then fff is integrable.

Proof. Say fff is increasing (it is then bounded by f(a)f(a)f(a) and f(b)f(b)f(b)). On the uniform partition PnP_nPn​, Mk=f(xk)M_k = f(x_k)Mk​=f(xk​) and mk=f(xk−1)m_k = f(x_{k-1})mk​=f(xk−1​), so the sum telescopes:

U(f,Pn)−L(f,Pn)=b−an∑k=1n(f(xk)−f(xk−1))=(b−a)(f(b)−f(a))n.U(f, P_n) - L(f, P_n) = \frac{b - a}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\bigl(f(x_k) - f(x_{k-1})\bigr) = \frac{(b - a)\bigl(f(b) - f(a)\bigr)}{n}. U(f,Pn​)−L(f,Pn​)=nb−a​k=1∑n​(f(xk​)−f(xk−1​))=n(b−a)(f(b)−f(a))​.

This is smaller than any given ε\varepsilonε once nnn is large. ■\blacksquare■

A monotone function may have infinitely many jumps (for instance one at every 1/k1/k1/k), and it is still integrable.

Continuous functions

Theorem. If fff is continuous on [a,b][a, b][a,b], then fff is integrable.

Proof. A continuous function on the compact set [a,b][a, b][a,b] is bounded (EVT) and uniformly continuous (post 02). Let ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0. Choose δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 such that ∣x−y∣<δ\lvert x - y\rvert < \delta∣x−y∣<δ implies ∣f(x)−f(y)∣<εb−a\lvert f(x) - f(y)\rvert < \frac{\varepsilon}{b - a}∣f(x)−f(y)∣<b−aε​. Take any partition PPP with mesh <δ< \delta<δ. On each subinterval, fff attains its max and min (EVT again) at points sk,tks_k, t_ksk​,tk​ with ∣sk−tk∣<δ\lvert s_k - t_k\rvert < \delta∣sk​−tk​∣<δ, so Mk−mk=f(sk)−f(tk)<εb−aM_k - m_k = f(s_k) - f(t_k) < \frac{\varepsilon}{b - a}Mk​−mk​=f(sk​)−f(tk​)<b−aε​. Therefore

U(f,P)−L(f,P)=∑k=1n(Mk−mk) Δxk<εb−a∑k=1nΔxk=ε.■U(f, P) - L(f, P) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} (M_k - m_k)\,\Delta x_k < \frac{\varepsilon}{b - a}\sum_{k=1}^{n} \Delta x_k = \varepsilon. \qquad \blacksquare U(f,P)−L(f,P)=k=1∑n​(Mk​−mk​)Δxk​<b−aε​k=1∑n​Δxk​=ε.■

Common pitfall: plain continuity is not enough for this proof. You need one δ\deltaδ that works on every subinterval at once, which is exactly uniform continuity. That is why the theorem is stated on a closed, bounded interval.

Finitely many discontinuities

Theorem. If fff is bounded on [a,b][a, b][a,b] and continuous except at finitely many points, then fff is integrable.

Sketch. Say ∣f∣≤B\lvert f\rvert \leq B∣f∣≤B and the bad points are c1,…,cmc_1, \dots, c_mc1​,…,cm​. Put a small interval of length η\etaη around each cjc_jcj​. Their total contribution to U−LU - LU−L is at most 2B⋅mη2B \cdot m\eta2B⋅mη, which is small when η\etaη is. On the remaining closed intervals fff is continuous, so the previous theorem makes their contribution as small as you like. ■\blacksquare■

Changing a function at finitely many points does not change whether it is integrable, or the value of the integral.

Let D(x)=1D(x) = 1D(x)=1 if x∈Qx \in \mathbb{Q}x∈Q and D(x)=0D(x) = 0D(x)=0 otherwise, on [0,1][0, 1][0,1]. Every subinterval of positive length contains both rationals and irrationals (density of Q\mathbb{Q}Q and of the irrationals, post 00), so Mk=1M_k = 1Mk​=1 and mk=0m_k = 0mk​=0 for every kkk and every partition. Therefore U(D,P)=1U(D, P) = 1U(D,P)=1 and L(D,P)=0L(D, P) = 0L(D,P)=0 always, the upper integral is 111, the lower integral is 000, and DDD is not Riemann integrable.

A function that is integrable: Thomae

Thomae's function on [0,1][0, 1][0,1] is

T(x)={1/qif x=p/q in lowest terms with q≥1,0if x is irrational,T(x) = \begin{cases} 1/q & \text{if } x = p/q \text{ in lowest terms with } q \geq 1, \\ 0 & \text{if } x \text{ is irrational}, \end{cases} T(x)={1/q0​if x=p/q in lowest terms with q≥1,if x is irrational,​

with T(0)=1T(0) = 1T(0)=1 (as 0=0/10 = 0/10=0/1). It is continuous at every irrational and discontinuous at every rational (post 02). Even so:

The points where T(x)≥ε/2T(x) \geq \varepsilon/2T(x)≥ε/2 are the fractions p/qp/qp/q with q≤2/εq \leq 2/\varepsilonq≤2/ε; there are finitely many, say NNN. Chapter 5 — The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

Part 1: integrating then differentiating

Theorem (FTC, part 1). Let fff be integrable on [a,b][a, b][a,b] and define

F(x)=∫axf(t) dt,x∈[a,b].F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt, \qquad x \in [a, b]. F(x)=∫ax​f(t)dt,x∈[a,b].

Then FFF is continuous on [a,b][a, b][a,b] (in fact Lipschitz). If fff is continuous at c∈[a,b]c \in [a, b]c∈[a,b], then FFF is differentiable at ccc and F′(c)=f(c)F'(c) = f(c)F′(c)=f(c) (one-sided at an endpoint).

Proof. Let ∣f∣≤B\lvert f\rvert \leq B∣f∣≤B. For x<yx < yx<y, additivity and the bound give ∣F(y)−F(x)∣=∣∫xyf∣≤B(y−x)\lvert F(y) - F(x)\rvert = \left\lvert \int_x^y f\right\rvert \leq B(y - x)∣F(y)−F(x)∣=​∫xy​f​≤B(y−x). So FFF is Lipschitz, hence continuous.

Now let fff be continuous at ccc and ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0. Choose δ\deltaδ with ∣f(t)−f(c)∣<ε\lvert f(t) - f(c)\rvert < \varepsilon∣f(t)−f(c)∣<ε for ∣t−c∣<δ\lvert t - c\rvert < \delta∣t−c∣<δ. For 0<∣x−c∣<δ0 < \lvert x - c\rvert < \delta0<∣x−c∣<δ,

F(x)−F(c)x−c−f(c)=1x−c∫cx(f(t)−f(c)) dt,\frac{F(x) - F(c)}{x - c} - f(c) = \frac{1}{x - c}\int_c^x \bigl(f(t) - f(c)\bigr)\,dt, x−cF(x)−F(c)​−f(c)=x−c1​∫cx​(f(t)−f(c))dt,

and the right side has absolute value at most 1∣x−c∣⋅ε∣x−c∣=ε\frac{1}{\lvert x - c\rvert}\cdot \varepsilon \lvert x - c\rvert = \varepsilon∣x−c∣1​⋅ε∣x−c∣=ε. ■\blacksquare■

So every continuous function has an antiderivative. One famous use: define ln⁡x=∫1xdtt\ln x = \int_1^x \frac{dt}{t}lnx=∫1x​tdt​ for x>0x > 0x>0. Then FTC 1 gives ln⁡′(x)=1x\ln'(x) = \frac1xln′(x)=x1​ at once.

Worked example. Let G(x)=∫0x2cos⁡(t2) dtG(x) = \int_0^{x^2} \cos(t^2)\,dtG(x)=∫0x2​cos(t2)dt. With F(u)=∫0ucos⁡(t2) dtF(u) = \int_0^{u} \cos(t^2)\,dtF(u)=∫0u​cos(t2)dt, FTC 1 gives F′(u)=cos⁡(u2)F'(u) = \cos(u^2)F′(u)=cos(u2), and G(x)=F(x2)G(x) = F(x^2)G(x)=F(x2). By the chain rule (post 03),

Part 2: differentiating then integrating

Theorem (FTC, part 2). Let FFF be differentiable on [a,b][a, b][a,b] (one-sided at the endpoints) and suppose f=F′f = F'f=F′ is integrable on [a,b][a, b][a,b]. Then

∫abf=F(b)−F(a).\int_a^b f = F(b) - F(a). ∫ab​f=F(b)−F(a).

Proof. Take any partition PPP. Apply the Mean Value Theorem (post 03) to FFF on each [xk−1,xk][x_{k-1}, x_k][xk−1​,xk​]: there is tkt_ktk​ in the open subinterval with F(xk)−F(xk−1)=F′(tk)Δxk=f(tk)ΔxkF(x_k) - F(x_{k-1}) = F'(t_k)\Delta x_k = f(t_k)\Delta x_kF(xk​)−F(xk−1​)=F′(tk​)Δxk​=f(tk​)Δxk​. Summing, the left side telescopes:

F(b)−F(a)=∑k=1nf(tk) Δxk.F(b) - F(a) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} f(t_k)\,\Delta x_k. F(b)−F(a)=k=1∑n​f(tk​)Δxk​.

Since mk≤f(tk)≤Mkm_k \leq f(t_k) \leq M_kmk​≤f(tk​)≤Mk​, this gives L(f,P)≤F(b)−F(a)≤U(f,P)L(f, P) \leq F(b) - F(a) \leq U(f, P)L(f,P)≤F(b)−F(a)≤U(f,P) for every PPP. So F(b)−F(a)F(b) - F(a)F(b)−F(a) lies between the lower and upper integrals, which are equal. ■\blacksquare■

Watch out: the hypothesis "F′F'F′ is integrable" cannot be dropped. F(x)=x2sin⁡(1/x2)F(x) = x^2\sin(1/x^2)F(x)=x2sin(1/x2) with F(0)=0F(0) = 0F(0)=0 is differentiable on [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1], but F′(x)=2xsin⁡(1/x2)−2xcos⁡(1/x2)F'(x) = 2x\sin(1/x^2) - \frac{2}{x}\cos(1/x^2)F′(x)=2xsin(1/x2)−x2​cos(1/x2) for x≠0x \neq 0x=0 is unbounded near 000, so it is not Riemann integrable. Integration by parts. If u,vu, vu,v are differentiable on [a,b][a, b][a,b] and u′,v′u', v'u′,v′ are integrable, then

∫abu v′=u(b)v(b)−u(a)v(a)−∫abu′ v.\int_a^b u\,v' = u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) - \int_a^b u'\,v. ∫ab​uv′=u(b)v(b)−u(a)v(a)−∫ab​u′v.

Chapter 6 — Improper integrals

The Riemann integral needs a bounded function on a closed, bounded interval. An improper integral relaxes one of these by a limit.

  • Unbounded interval. If fff is integrable on [a,R][a, R][a,R] for every R>aR > aR>a, define ∫a∞f=lim⁡R→∞∫aRf\int_a^\infty f = \lim_{R \to \infty} \int_a^R f∫a∞​f=limR→∞​∫aR​f when the limit exists (the integral converges).
  • Unbounded function. If fff is integrable on [a+η,b][a + \eta, b][a+η,b] for every small η>0\eta > 0η>0, define ∫abf=lim⁡η→0+∫a+ηbf\int_a^b f = \lim_{\eta \to 0^+} \int_{a+\eta}^b f∫ab​f=limη→0+​∫a+ηb​f.

The p-test. For p>0p > 0p>0:

∫1Rx−p dx={1−R1−pp−1p≠1,ln⁡Rp=1.\int_1^R x^{-p}\,dx = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1 - R^{1-p}}{p - 1} & p \neq 1, \\ \ln R & p = 1. \end{cases} ∫1R​x−pdx=⎩⎨⎧​p−11−R1−p​lnR​p=1,p=1.​

Chapter 7 — Lebesgue's criterion, and why Lebesgue integration exists

Measure zero

A set A⊆RA \subseteq \mathbb{R}A⊆R has measure zero if for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 it can be covered by countably many open intervals whose total length is less than ε\varepsilonε.

  • Every finite set has measure zero.
  • Every countable set {a1,a2,… }\{a_1, a_2, \dots\}{a1​,a2​,…} has measure zero: cover aka_kak​ by an interval of length ε/2k+1\varepsilon/2^{k+1}ε/2k+1; the total is at most ε/2\varepsilon/2ε/2. So Q\mathbb{Q}Q has measure zero (it is countable, post 00).
  • An interval [c,d][c, d][c,d] with c<dc < dc<d does not have measure zero.

Theorem (Lebesgue's criterion). A function f:[a,b]→Rf : [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}f:[a,b]→R is Riemann integrable if and only if fff is bounded and the set of points where fff is discontinuous has measure zero.

This explains every example in the post at once:

Function Discontinuities Integrable?
continuous fff none yes
monotone fff countable (jumps) yes
Thomae TTT the rationals: countable yes
Dirichlet DDD every point of [0,1][0, 1][0,1] no
x−1/2x^{-1/2}x−1/2 on (0,1](0, 1](0,1] — but unbounded not Riemann; only improper

The proof is in Abbott, Section 7.6, and Rudin, Theorem 11.33.

Why a better integral was needed

The Riemann integral does not behave well under limits. Enumerate the rationals in [0,1][0, 1][0,1] as q1,q2,…q_1, q_2, \dotsq1​,q2​,… and let fnf_nfn​ be 111 at q1,…,qnq_1, \dots, q_nq1​,…,qn​ and 000 elsewhere. Each fnf_nfn​ has finitely many discontinuities, so it is integrable with ∫01fn=0\int_0^1 f_n = 0∫01​fn​=0. The functions increase and are bounded by 111, and fn(x)→D(x)f_n(x) \to D(x)fn​(x)→D(x) at every xxx. But the limit DDD is not Riemann integrable, so "∫fn→∫lim⁡fn\int f_n \to \int \lim f_n∫fn​→∫limfn​" is not even meaningful.

Lebesgue's integral (1902) partitions the range of fff instead of its domain, and measures the sets where fff takes values in each range slice. It integrates DDD (answer 000, since Q\mathbb{Q}Q has measure zero), agrees with the Riemann integral whenever the latter exists, and satisfies clean limit theorems such as the Monotone and Dominated Convergence Theorems. Post 05 shows the Riemann-world substitute: limits and integrals commute when convergence is uniform.

Exercise 7. Explain why the pointwise limit of integrable functions need not be integrable, using the functions fnf_nfn​ from Chapter 7.

Solution

Each fnf_nfn​ is 111 at nnn rationals and 000 elsewhere, so it has nnn discontinuities and ∫01fn=0\int_0^1 f_n = 0∫01​fn​=0. What's next

Post 05 studies sequences and series of functions. It separates pointwise from uniform convergence, proves that uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous and that integrals commute with uniform limits (the theorem the Dirichlet example above was missing), and then applies everything to power series: radius of convergence, term-by-term differentiation and integration, Abel's theorem and the Weierstrass approximation theorem.

  • Michael Spivak, Calculus, 4th ed., Publish or Perish, 2008 — Chapters 13–14 (integrals and the Fundamental Theorem).
  • Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis I: Introduction to Real Analysis, free textbook — jirka.org/ra, Chapter 5.
  • MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.100A Real Analysis (Fall 2020), lecture notes on the Riemann integral and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

Note: this post is in progress. Planned additions: the Riemann–Stieltjes integral, a full proof of Lebesgue's criterion, the integral test with its error bounds, and the integral form of the Taylor remainder from post 03.
